latin.601: §. XXI. Waldensium tàm Veterum, quàm Novorum, de Sacra Cœna sententia, etsi quandoque (quod citatis retrò Theologis Lutheranis facile dabimus) obscurius proposita, SECULO XVII ad istam tamen potissimum Protestantium, i.e. Papismum oppugnantium, partem transiit, quæ REFORMATORUM nomine hodieque venit.
latin.602: Probant id tam Confessiones horum publicæ, quam Privatorum Doctorum celebriorum Scripta, adhuc novissimè ex Harmonia Confessionum aliisque eorum Libris, collecta & recensita, tùm à Reformato Cosino, Episcopo Dunelmensi, in Historia Transsubstantiationis Papalis, cap. 2. integro, tùm à Lutherano Abbate Lutherensi, Doctore & Professore Helmstadiensi in Consideratione Controversiarum à pag. 492. ad pag. seq.
latin.603: vindicata insuper ab horum priori §. XIII., ex Scriptis Buceri Anglicis, Zwinglii & Tigurinorum veterum sententiâ, quà modum loquendi æquè atque quà Rem & veritatem, Berengarium studiosius & ad superstitionem usque æmulantium, intereà cum ipso etiam Luthero quàm facillimè conciliandorum, quemadmodum id latius & ex professo evicimus in præfatione ad scripta Buceri Eucharistica, propediem in luci publica redonanda parag. 15.
latin.604: Hộc locô in superpondium doctrinæ & Fidei de præsentia corporis Christi, in S. Cœna, realissima, utut spirituali, tam Confessionibus Reformatorum publicis, quàm privatorum Doctorum Scriptis, quin in Ecclesiis nostris Germanicis, Laici cujusvis adstipulationi quotidianæ, receptæ & frequentatæ, adjicimus efficacissimas quasdam expressiones Liturgicas, tàm ante, quam post administratam apud eos in Germania S. Cœnam, prælegi solitas, ipsis quoque precibus, ad Deum hoc tempore fundendis, insertas sequentes.
latin.605: Ante Administrationem quidem precesque, quando confitentur: Das Christus selbst (verstehe vornehmlich seinem gecreuzigtem Fleisch und vergossenem Blut nach) unseren hungerigen und durstigen Seelen / zur wahren Speiß und Tranck des ewigen Lebens worden sey. i. e. Christum ipsum (puta corpore præcipuè suô crucifixô & sanguine effusô) animabus nostris esurientibus ac sitientibus, in verum cibum potumque cedere. In precibus, administrationi præmissis, quando Deo supplicant: Daß ihre mühselige und zerschlagene Herzen / mit Christi wahrem Leib und Blut / ja mit ihm / wahren GOTT und Menschen / dem wahren Himmel Brodt / durch die Krafft des Heil. Geistes / gespeiset und erquicket werden. i. e. quò animæ suæ fatigatæ ac dilaceratæ, verô Christi corpore & sanguine, quin ipso totô, DEO verô homineque, æterno illo pane cœlesti vescantur ac refocillentur.
latin.606: Denique, post preces finitas, quando Communicantes in universum omnes graviter monemur: Daß wir mit unseren Herzen nicht an dem äusserlichen Brodt und Wein hafften sollen; Sondern unsere Herzen und Glauben gründen auff das Wort der Verheissung: Und nicht zweiffeln / daß wir so warhafftig / durch die Wirckung des Heiligen Geistes / mit des HERRN Leib und Blut / an unseren Seelen, gespeiset und getränket werden / als wir das heilige Brodt und Tranck zu seiner Gedächtniß empfangen. i. e. ne cordibus nostris animisque pani & vino, externis symbolis adhærescamus, sed mentes Fidemque in Verbis Promissionis defixas habeamus, nulli dubitantes, nos non minus verè, per operationem Spiritûs S. ipsissimo Domini Salvatoris corpore & sanguine, quà animas nostras, escari potarique, quàm panem consecratum potumque in commemorationem Christi accipimus.

pass_a.601: §. XXI. The sentence of the Waldenses, both Old and New, concerning the Sacred Supper — although sometimes proposed more obscurely (which we will easily grant to the Lutheran Theologians cited above) — yet in the XVIIth AGE passed over to that most potent part of the Protestants, i.e. of those opposing Papism, which to this day comes under the name of the REFORMED.
pass_a.602: This is proved both by these men’s public Confessions and by the Writings of more celebrated Private Doctors, still most recently collected and reviewed from the Harmony of Confessions and their other Books — both by the Reformed Cosin, Bishop of Durham, in the History of Papal Transubstantiation, the whole of ch. 2, and by the Lutheran Abbot of Lutheren, Doctor and Professor at Helmstedt, in the Consideration of Controversies from p. 492 to the following page.
pass_a.603: further vindicated from these men’s prior §. XIII., from Bucer’s English Writings and the sentence of Zwingli and the old Tigurines — who as to manner of speaking equally and as to the Thing and truth more studiously and even to superstition emulated Berengar — meanwhile most easily to be reconciled even with Luther himself, as we have more largely and expressly proved in the preface to Bucer’s Eucharistic writings, soon to be restored to public light, parag. 15.
pass_a.604: In this place, as a superweight of the doctrine and Faith concerning the presence of Christ’s body in the Sacred Supper — most real, though spiritual — we add to the Reformed’s public Confessions and private Doctors’ Writings, and even to any layman’s daily received and frequented assent in our German Churches, certain most efficacious Liturgical expressions, accustomed to be read both before and after the Sacred Supper administered among them in Germany, inserted also in the prayers to be poured out to God at this time, as follows.
pass_a.605: Before the Administration and the prayers, when they confess: That Christ Himself (understand chiefly as to His crucified Flesh and poured-out Blood) has become to our hungry and thirsty souls the true Food and Drink of eternal Life — i.e. that Christ Himself (namely chiefly by His crucified body and poured-out blood) yields to our hungering and thirsting souls as true food and drink. In the prayers preceding administration, when they supplicate God: That their toilsome and crushed hearts may be fed and refreshed with Christ’s true Body and Blood — yes with Him, true GOD and Man, the true Bread of Heaven — through the power of the Holy Spirit — i.e. that their fatigued and torn souls may feed and be refreshed with Christ’s true body and blood, nay with Him whole, true GOD and man, that eternal heavenly bread.
pass_a.606: Finally, after the prayers are finished, when we Communicants all in common are gravely warned: That we should not cling with our hearts to the outward Bread and Wine; But ground our hearts and Faith on the Word of Promise: And not doubt that we are as truly, through the working of the Holy Spirit, fed and given to drink with the LORD’s Body and Blood at our souls as we receive the holy Bread and Drink in His remembrance — i.e. that we should not adhere with our hearts and minds to bread and wine, the external symbols, but keep minds and Faith fixed on the Words of Promise, doubting nothing that we are no less truly, by the Holy Spirit’s operation, fed and given to drink as to our souls with the Lord Savior’s very own body and blood than we receive the consecrated bread and drink in remembrance of Christ.

601: §.XXI: the Waldenses’ Supper sentence — old and new — is sometimes obscure (as the Lutheran critics said), yet in Age XVII it passed to the chief anti-papal Protestant wing.
That wing still bears the name REFORMED.
602: Proof stands in the Reformed public confessions and celebrated private doctors’ writings — freshly gathered from the Harmony of Confessions and related books.
Cosin (Durham) treats it in his History of Papal Transubstantiation ch. 2 entire; the Lutheran Helmstedt abbot in Consideration of Controversies from p. 492 on.
603: Further vindication (their prior §.XIII): Bucer’s English writings and old Zwingli/Tigurine sentence — eager even to superstition after Berengar’s manner of speech and the Thing itself.
Yet they are most easily reconciled even with Luther — as Strimesius showed at large in the preface to Bucer’s Eucharistic writings (§15).
604: Here, as superweight for the most real though spiritual presence of Christ’s body in the Supper, add not only public confessions and private writings,
but the German churches’ daily lay assent — and the most efficacious liturgical expressions read before and after the Supper in Germany, inserted in the prayers of the hour.
605: Before administration they confess: Christ Himself — chiefly as crucified flesh and poured blood — has become true food and drink of eternal life to hungry, thirsty souls.
In the preceding prayers they ask that crushed hearts be fed and refreshed with Christ’s true Body and Blood — yes with Him, true God and Man, heaven’s bread — by the Holy Spirit’s power.
606: After the prayers, communicants are warned: do not cling to outward bread and wine; ground heart and faith on the Word of Promise.

Doubt not that by the Spirit’s working we are as truly fed and given drink at our souls with the Lord’s Body and Blood as we receive the holy bread and cup in His remembrance. Stop before the next § (spiritual-presence modes digression).
